subsections.subsection_title: 2.1 Additive Correction of a Fixed Predictor
subsections.methodology_cluster: Fixed-slope intercept estimation and constant residual correction
subsections.sota_investigation_mission: Find specialized papers and technical reports on adding a scalar offset to an otherwise fixed predictor, including recent relevant work published by 2026-11. Identify their assumptions and estimation protocols for conceptual context. Do not propose additional methods to beat or imply that any external method was evaluated.
subsections.limitation_hypothesis: The supplied baseline has no added intercept and therefore leaves the constant residual 3 on every supplied observation. A scalar correction changes only this offset; the inputs provide no evidence about correcting other residual patterns or other observations.
subsections.bridge_to_our_method: Explain that the supplied calculation obtains b=mean(y-2x)=3 and adds it to the fixed predictor. It exactly removes the observed constant residual on the five supplied points; it establishes no broader resolution of limitations reported elsewhere.

subsections.sota_investigation_mission: Find specialized technical sources on mean absolute error, mean squared error, and the interpretation of errors evaluated on observations used for estimation. subsections.limitation_hypothesis: The correction is determined and evaluated on identical observations. Consequently, the recorded zero errors cannot establish held-out predictive performance. The deterministic log also supplies no basis for uncertainty estimates or statistical significance claims.
subsections.bridge_to_our_method: The teaching note addresses interpretation through explicit protocol disclosure: show the complete observations, correction calculation, and recorded error table, and state that all numerical conclusions concern those same five points. The protocol does not resolve the absence of held-out evaluation.

Specify x=[-2,-1,0,1,2], targets y=2x+3, baseline predictions 2x, and corrected predictions 2x+b from idea.md and experimental_log.md.
Define each observed residual as y-2x and compute the five residuals as [3,3,3,3,3].
Define mean absolute error as the sum of the five absolute prediction residuals divided by 5, and mean squared error as the sum of their squares divided by 5.
